sub: Put three dates side by side before approving the hire.
q: Which date is hardest to estimate?
alt: Timeline: payroll begins first, productive capacity and customer payments arrive later; the interval is labelled cash carries the gap.
note: Illustrative timing. Your dates depend on your inputs.

sub: Hold everything else fixed. See what moves.
listlabel: PICK ONE · KEEP THE REST FIXED
q: Which assumption do you challenge first?
alt: Three candidate assumptions to test one at a time: fewer customers, slower ramp-up, later collections.

sub: Write the stop conditions before you read the forecast.
items: A cash balance you won't go below
alt: Three decision boundaries: a minimum cash balance, a commitment you cannot unwind, demand you need evidence for.

sub: Price $100, variable cost $60. A 10% discount cuts contribution from $40 to $30.
foot: ≈33% more sales needed to recover the same total contribution
q: Can your capacity carry the extra volume?
alt: Illustrative comparison: contribution per sale falls from $40 to $30 after a 10% discount, requiring about 33% more sales.
note: Illustrative example. Assumes variable cost, capacity and fixed costs stay unchanged.

sub: One client pays before delivery. One pays after.
foot: If payroll and suppliers come first, the business finances the gap
q: Which payment term pressures your team most?
alt: Two clients buying the same service: one pays before delivery, one pays after completion, creating a financing gap.

sub: Add a four-line decision note to every model.
items: The assumptions that could change it
The next action — and its owner
alt: A four-line decision note: the decision, the assumptions that could change it, missing evidence, and the next action with an owner.

sub: A temporary spike can create a permanent payroll commitment.
gap: HOW LONG CAN YOU CARRY IT?
q: What evidence turns a busy month into a hire?
alt: Timeline: bookings spike, a hire starts, bookings return to normal while payroll continues.

sub: Deposits and payments can start before useful output.
q: Which cost before productive use is easiest to miss?
alt: Timeline: equipment deposit and financing payments begin before the equipment reaches useful output.

sub: Compare the cost of learning with what it can resolve.
foot: Sometimes the smaller test is too expensive or unrepresentative to help
alt: Comparison of a full expansion, hard to reverse, with a pilot or phased option that tests demand first.

sub: Inputs can look equally precise and rest on very different foundations.
q: Which input would you investigate first?
alt: Three inputs ranked by evidence: paid invoices strong, supplier quote medium, customers not yet won is an assumption.

sub: Use the first site as evidence — not as a copy.
items: Who runs it day to day?
q: Which assumption would you refuse to copy?
alt: Three questions for a second location: whether demand transfers, who runs it, and how long it takes to reach useful capacity.

sub: A personal walkthrough for advisors working on a hire, equipment purchase or expansion.
alt: Invitation for advisors to a personal AIWMC Quantis walkthrough of an illustrative decision.
